newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe line may harden in transatlantic gene-soya row.
newsitem.headline: Europe line may harden in transatlantic gene-soya row.

text.p: Markets for oilseeds in Europe were rethinking their line on genetically-altered soybeans which American farmers will start supplying in a few weeks.
They were reacting to a multi-country protest organised by environmentalist group Greenpeace, which seeks to force food companies to boycott the products, or provide clear labels.

"General indifference seems to have given way to a belief that labelling of soya products or of entire United States soybean cargos would be the best response to quell public concerns and to avoid a harmful boycott," a broker said.
"It's still unclear whether this will die down or if it will blow up into a major food industry war with consumers."
So-called crushers, who process oilseeds to make vegetable oil for some 30,000 food products such as margarine as well as meals for animal feed, were initially unfazed by protests.
They believed American assurances the new products were safe and a segregation in production and transport impossible.
Europe is heavily dependent on soybeans, which make up more than half of all oilseeds processed here. The United States supply 60 percent of the total.
The Brussels oil mill lobby FEDIOL now thinks labels are a good idea if they are clear and practicable.

"Greenpeace wants labelling and what the EU Commission should give them is a compromise, maybe the scare is legitimate after all the health scares we've had over the past years," said director general Pascale Cogels from Brussels.
"Let people reflect on that, give them a choice, and maybe they won't care anymore as they see the products are safe."
"Authorities should be told they should be careful about these products and do their duty in assessing them."
Greenpeace activists today attached banners on buildings of leading soya products processor, food manufacturer Unilever demanding consumers be given more choice.
Consumers cannot avoid soya and therefore would have to eat genetically-altered food unknowingly, they said.
Developed by American firm Monsanto Co, the new products which have been made resistant to a weed-killer, have been declared safe by health authorities in the United States, Europe and Japan.
But Greenpeace says dangers of allergic reactions cannot be ruled out and the impact on the environment is unknown.
A European Parliament committee later today will discuss how precise the labels should be.
Legislators think only substantial changes to a product should be printed on a label, but this would not include oil and meal from genetically-altered beans after they have been processed.
Consumer lobbies want to know where products come from and whether or not they are derived from gene-altered organisms.
But Cogels warned, "Oil heated during crushing of traditional beans is identical with oil made from genetically-altered beans as the minute traces of modified protein are destroyed."
"If you label these products separately you won't be able to check -- you'd give rise to fraud and market distortions."
As soy oil has lost favour since the row erupted, domestic rapeseed oil has risen to an untypical price premium.
Traders said radical market participants saw Latin American soybeans replacing North American supplies and palm oil and sunseed oil making up for soy oil shortages if it came to a boycott.
Soymeal in animal feeding could be replaced by feed grain.
But the EU could lose crucial export markets for the soy oil it produces by using American beans.
